speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: At that time, we explained that the Act had three key objectives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Our CIIs are core computer systems that, if disrupted, could affect our national security and survival and were thus important to secure first.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Second, to authorise the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore, or CSA, to lead in the prevention and response to cybersecurity threats and incidents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: And third, to establish a licensing framework to regulate cybersecurity service providers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: In 2018, we saw that there was a need for stronger regulatory levers to safeguard our national cybersecurity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: At that time, we were one of the first jurisdictions in the world to introduce cybersecurity legislation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: The Cybersecurity Act has now been in force for six years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: The core objectives continue to be relevant today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: We have reviewed the Act, learning from our experiences and taking into account changes in technology.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: We have made progress and, in certain areas, we lead in cybersecurity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: This has allowed us to play a useful role in international efforts to address cybersecurity challenges.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: For example, Singapore has been chairing the United Nations Open-Ended Working Group (OEWG) on Security of and in the Use of Information and Communications Technologies since 2021.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: The five-year OEWG is the only UN forum for discussions on cybersecurity and norms for responsible state behaviour in cyberspace.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: OEWG is also part of the reason why Minister Josephine Teo cannot be here today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: She is currently in the US to participate in and lend her support to OEWG-related discussions, amongst other engagements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: In order to continue to ensure Singapore's cybersecurity, a review and an update to the Act is needed as several aspects of our operating context have changed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Technology has evolved and, as a result, business models have changed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Cloud computing, as a service, has become widely available and widely used.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: When the Act was first written, it was the norm for CII to be physical systems held on premises and entirely owned or controlled by the CII owner.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: But the advent of cloud services has challenged this model.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Key benefits of digitalisation are scale and aggregation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Today, it is possible to aggregate and share common digital services and functions across borders to deliver essential services in different countries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: This has likewise challenged us to review how we can safeguard the cybersecurity of our essential services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Malicious actors are increasingly finding new ways to their target, such as through supply chain attacks or starting with adjacent systems.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: One example Members may be familiar with is the SolarWinds cybersecurity breach in 2020, where a network management software that was widely used by major companies worldwide was compromised.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: The attacker used the software's regular updates to implant a backdoor and gain a foothold in the networks of organisations that downloaded and installed the malicious update, and then this provided the attacker with privileged access to internal networks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Digital technology is now an integral part of our lives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: In Singapore, over 90% of residents now communicate online.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: More of us are now online for longer and online for more varied purposes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: This means that we are exposed to more cyber risks, as every digital technology we use, every transaction we make and every connection made between computers, is a possible route for attack.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: The cybersecurity professionals refer to this as an increased "attack surface".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: To cause significant disruption to the way we work and live, those who mean us harm can take down the digital infrastructure we depend on, or the institutions and entities that hold our sensitive information or perform functions of national interest.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Hence, when it comes to securing Singapore in cyberspace, regulating the cybersecurity or CIIs is no longer sufficient.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: It is vital that we update our cybersecurity laws to continue to stay ahead of the curve.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Other jurisdictions like Australia, the European Union (EU), Malaysia, the United Kingdom (UK) and the United States (US) have also been grappling with these developments and the ensuing implications on how to do cybersecurity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: These jurisdictions have also recently introduced or announced plans to have new cybersecurity legislation to address these same concerns.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Additionally, having had the experience of operationalising the Act and engaging with multiple stakeholders over the last six years, we have received feedback and we have learnt many lessons on how we can better implement and enforce the Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: These included our CII owners, cybersecurity and legal professionals, academic experts, sector regulators, industry players, trade associations and chambers, and members of the public.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Stakeholders have generally been supportive of our proposed Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: They understand the need for stronger cybersecurity regulation and are supportive of the policy objectives of the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Our stakeholders have also provided useful feedback that has helped CSA refine the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: It is not in Singapore's national security interests to do so, as public disclosure of these systems and entities may expose them to more risks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: The list of CIIs is not made public.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Similarly, systems and entities regulated pursuant to the proposed amendments will also not be made public.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: The 2018 Act was developed to regulate CIIs that were physical systems, but new technology and business models have emerged since.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Hence, we need to update the Act to allow us to better regulate CIIs so that they continue to be secure and resilient against cyber threats, whatever technology or business model they run on.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: The Bill will do this in the following ways.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Clause 3(j) also introduces provisions setting out what "ownership" means in relation to virtual computers or computer systems.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Currently, the Act's definitions of "computer" and "computer system" are predicated on them being physical computers that are built out of dedicated physical hardware, such as hard disk drives, memory and processor chips.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: This was suitable in 2018, as CIIs were physical systems.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: However, given recent technological advancements, it is now possible that a CII could be a virtual computer system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Our interest is in the computer or computer system that is necessary for the continuous delivery of the essential service, whether it is physical or virtual.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: However, in the case of a virtual CII, such as in a cloud environment, the underlying physical infrastructure could be shared or easily replace, and, therefore, it would not be sensible or meaningful to regulate the underlying hardware.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: The new definitions we are introducing allow us to make it clear that the CII owner is responsible for the cybersecurity of its virtualised CII, and not other parties that supply the underlying physical infrastructure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: This will deal with situations where a provider of an essential service could leverage a computer system owned by a third party because it would be more effective or efficient to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: For example, hypothetically, a third-party vendor could own, operate and supply a critical Operations Management system that is used by multiple providers of a given essential service.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: The third-party vendor could have greater expertise operating such a system and is able to do so at a lower cost, due to demand aggregation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: The principal Act did not provide for such business models because it was the norm then for providers of essential services to own and operate their critical systems.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Business models may be changing but the fundamental principle remains the same.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Providers of essential services must remain responsible for the cybersecurity and cyber resilience of the computer systems relied upon to deliver essential services that they provide.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: The new Part 3A will ensure that they cannot outsource this responsibility even if they rely on a third party's computer system for the continuous delivery of the essential service.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Under the new Part 3A, the responsibility rests with the provider of essential service.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: To be clear, CSA does not seek to regulate the owners of these systems under Part 3A, who are the third-party vendors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: However, the providers of essential services must ensure that the systems they rely on can meet comparable cybersecurity standards and requirements of a CII through legally binding commitments, such as contracts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Third-party vendors that seek to work with providers of essential services will need to have the necessary expertise and capability to own and operate a CII in a manner that meets the cybersecurity standards we hold a CII to.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: It is a specialised area and a considered business decision to operate in this space.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Members will appreciate that not many businesses will be, nor can be, in this space.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Clause 8 allows CSA to deal with situations where a CII is supporting an essential service from overseas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: The Act currently only allows CSA to designate computers or computer systems as CII if the entire or part of the computer or computer system is in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: However, this has also meant that CSA is currently unable to regulate a CII that is wholly located overseas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: We will also be updating CII-related provisions to address the inventiveness of malicious cyber actors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Under the principal Act, a CII owner is generally only obliged to report cybersecurity incidents relating to the CII, or computers or computer systems that are interconnected with or communicate with the CII.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: CSA needs such incident reporting so that it can intervene early if necessary and gain better situational awareness so that it can proactively alert other sectors and prevent the spread of similar attacks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: As the tactics and techniques of malicious actors evolve to target systems at the periphery or along the supply chains, we must also start placing our alarms at those places.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: The former requirement will help us be better prepared should any of our essential services be targeted in the same manner as in the SolarWinds case.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: The latter requirement will enable us to take proactive steps to protect our CIIs, if CII owners' immediate suppliers are compromised, to pre-empt potential disruptions to our essential services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: The requirement to report on incidents affecting immediate suppliers will apply only if the CII is owned by the provider of essential service.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: In situations where a third party owns the CII, the provider of essential service is unlikely to have visibility of the third party's suppliers to be able to report any incident to CSA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: We will also expand the Act to regulate a new type of system called Systems of Temporary Cybersecurity Concern, or STCC, so as to address the evolution of our threat landscape.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic drove home the importance of being able to secure such systems.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: During the pandemic, many governments around the world developed temporary systems to support the tracking and distribution of vaccinations and many of these systems were targeted by malicious actors seeking to exploit the urgency of the situation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Should we be faced with another national pandemic, we need to be in the position to secure the systems critical to our crisis response.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Another potential group of STCCs could include systems supporting high-key international events in Singapore, such as the Trump-Kim Summit in 2018, or the Youth Olympic Games in 2010.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Such international events could be attractive targets for cyber-malicious actors seeking a global stage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: The Tokyo Olympics of 2021, for example, was reported to have encountered 450 million cyber-attacks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: We need to take the cybersecurity of such events seriously to maintain Singapore's reputation as a safe and reliable place to host such events.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Before the Commissioner of Cybersecurity can designate a system as an STCC, the Commissioner must be satisfied that, for a limited period, the system is at high risk of a cybersecurity threat or incident; and the loss or compromise of the system will have a serious detrimental effect on the national security, defence, foreign relations, economy, public health, public safety, or public order of Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: In other words, this is intended to apply to systems that are critical to Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Given that STCCs are critical systems when they are set up, Part 3B will impose on STCC owners' cybersecurity obligations similar to those for CII owners, where practicable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Part 3B will allow CSA to be proactive in raising the cybersecurity posture of the STCC, depending on the operating context and the time period for which the STCC is needed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: These entities will be referred to as Entities of Special Cybersecurity Interest, or ESCIs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: One example of potential ESCIs could be universities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Universities are popular targets of malicious actors, given their standing in society, the sensitive research they may do, and the data they may possess.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: For instance, in 2019, the Australian National University detected a database breach, reportedly by a state actor, which resulted in unauthorised access to extensive personal information, including bank records, tax details and passport information of students and staff dating back almost two decades.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Senior Australian officials feared that such data could be used to exploit or recruit students and alumni as informants.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Our own universities have also been targets of cyber-attacks in the past.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: The Ministry of Education and the universities have since taken steps to strengthen their cybersecurity defences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: The proposed amendments in this Bill could further strengthen our universities' defences and enable CSA to take stronger action to secure them as well as other entities of special cybersecurity interest if they are designated.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: However, the specific list of entities designated as ESCIs should not be disclosed publicly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: This is to avoid inadvertently advertising these entities as worthy targets to malicious actors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: ESCIs will be required to report prescribed cybersecurity incidents that result in a breach of the availability, confidentiality, or integrity of the entities' data, or have a significant impact on the business operations of the entities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: CSA will also be empowered to issue written directions to ESCIs, if necessary or expedient, for ensuring the cybersecurity of the ESCIs or the effective administration of the Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: The obligations we impose on ESCIs will be moderated when compared to those imposed on CIIs or STCCs, in recognition that the impact on our national interest resulting from cyber-attacks on ESCIs may not be as severe compared to the impact from cyber-attacks on CIIs or STCCs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: This ensures that regulatory obligations are commensurate with the cybersecurity risks posed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Our ability to operate normally and to enable citizens to meet their day-to-day needs has become increasingly dependent on the good functioning of the digital infrastructure that powers our digital economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: The more foundational the digital infrastructure is to systems central to our work and lives, the more attractive it is to malicious actors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Infrastructural vulnerabilities can be exploited to compromise many systems and can cause widespread disruption.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: The new Part 3D will allow CSA to regulate major providers of FDI service for cybersecurity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: This refers to entities that serve a large number of businesses or organisations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: This reflects our interest in securing ourselves against the risk of widespread disruption or deterioration of activities that rely on or are enabled by the FDI service.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: This also means that smaller players, who are more sensitive to regulatory costs, will not be regulated.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: These major providers must be providers of FDI services specified in the new Third Schedule, which will be introduced by clause 30.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: The digital world moves quickly, so our approach must allow for quick adaptation and agility.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: As new types of digital infrastructure grow in importance to our needs, they can be added to the new Third Schedule.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Recognising that major FDI service providers provide services to clients across sectors and often across borders, CSA has been consulting closely with industry and sector leads to develop inter-operable standards, codes and operating parameters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: We are mindful about compliance costs for these major providers and are committed to keeping them reasonable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: The same appeal avenues available to those designated as CII owners under the Act today will be extended to providers of essential services under Part 3A, STCC owners, ESCI and major FDI service providers that CSA designates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: For example, any entity that receives a designation notice may appeal against the designation and regulated entities can appeal CSA's decisions, orders and directions as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: This is encapsulated in the new section 35B introduced by clause 19.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: The proposed stop in the Bill is targeted and affects only providers of essential services, owners of STCCs, ESCIs and major FDI providers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: There are a known and finite set, and CSA has been and will be working closely with them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: The Bill does not impose cybersecurity obligations on the larger business community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: We will also enhance the Act to strengthen the administration of the Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: To improve CSA's ability to enforce the Act against recalcitrant CII owners regulated under Part 3 of the Act, clause 13(b) will amend section 15(4) to empower CSA to inspect the CII if it appears to the Commissioner that the CII owner has not complied with its obligations or has provided information requested under section 10 of the Act that is false, misleading, inaccurate, or incomplete.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: This is because wilful non-compliance by CII owners could jeopardise our national security and survival.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Currently, Part 5 of the Act regulates persons who provide licensable cybersecurity services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Clause 18 will provide monitoring powers for licensing officers, for the purposes of executing Part 5.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: In the absence of such powers, CSA could face difficulties in seeking information from uncooperative licensed cybersecurity service providers to verify their compliance with the conditions of their licences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: The new provisions will give CSA powers of entry and inspection, and to require the production of records, accounts and documents from licensed cybersecurity service providers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Non-compliance with such requirements without reasonable excuse will be a criminal offence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: While we seek to strengthen CSA's ability to act and enforce the law as the national cybersecurity authority, we recognise that there are criminals looking to exploit this authority through impersonation scams.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Clause 22 allows the Commissioner to grant an extension of time to any person required to do any action under relevant parts of the Act, as long as there are good reasons to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: This was borne out of our experience where there were valid reasons, at times, for regulated entities to not be able to comply with the obligations of the Act under business-as-usual timelines.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: Thus, the Bill also recommends a key revision to the penalties that can be imposed for non-compliance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: In the current Act, non-compliance with statutory obligations in relation to CII is to be enforced through criminal penalties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: This was appropriate as the measures imposed on CII in the 2018 Act are needed to ensure their cybersecurity and in turn the undisrupted delivery of our essential services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: We needed to underscore the gravity if there was any non-compliance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: This Bill before the House today will introduce more obligations on CII owners under the existing Part 3, such as the new reporting requirements relating to peripheral systems, as well as the proposed provisions covering new classes of systems and entities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: In making a recommendation to the Public Prosecutor, CSA will consider a range of factors, including the risks created by the non-compliance, egregiousness and facts of the case.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: This Bill will strengthen our cybersecurity, and increase trust in using online services in Singapore in our highly digitalised nation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: It is calibrated to address the risks to the nation, our economy and our way of life while balancing compliance costs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: In implementing the proposed new laws, our experience with the 2018 Act will serve us well and we will continue to refine our approach in consultation with stakeholders and consider new international best practices as they emerge.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
text: With that, Mr Speaker, I beg to move.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Major sectors such as finance, healthcare and infocomm underwent significant transformations over the past two decades.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In the 2000s, the world saw a surge in internet usage with more than one billion people on the Internet in 2005.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Over the two decades, technology continues to advance in many ways.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At the same time, with the proliferation of smart phones and wide range of apps, people essentially carry a mini-computer as they move, signifying technology has become more personal and portable.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Advances in cloud computing also changed the way organisations are structured and how global business operations are carried out.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Established enterprises have been harnessing cloud technologies to streamline operations, enhance scalability and reduce costs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Many new startups that are "born in the cloud" are basically cloud-enabled by design.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These developments demonstrate how technology touches nearly everything we do and how digitally interconnected we are today.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, unlike in the past when transactions and important activities can be physically siloed, systems are now highly interconnected and workers can access work systems, links and files via their smart phones and consumer grade apps, possibly with lower standards of security safeguards.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These present many opportunities or larger attacks surface for bad actors to launch cyber-attacks from anywhere in the world, from different angles and with new sophistication.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: A moment of carelessness can open up the entire network or system to attacks.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, I fully concur with the three shifts that the Senior Minister of State highlighted in his opening speech earlier and the need to strengthen the Cybersecurity Act accordingly.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I also agree in principle with the consequential amendments set out in this Bill.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, I do have some clarifications that I would like to seek from the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In the Senior Minister of State's speech earlier, he indicated that the CII owner will only need to report incidents involving immediate suppliers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In view of the highly dynamic operating environment and tight manpower situation, how will the CSA ensure that it is not overly onerous on the CII owners?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Conversely, with this expanded coverage, will the CSA be able to cope with the expected increase in incident reports?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Mandating incident reports as part of enhancing detection is critical, but the ability to act on the issues and risks presented in a timely manner is just as critical.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Otherwise, introducing this new requirement to enhance CSA's situational awareness will defeat its purpose.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As business operations change and cross-border supply of services is now highly prevalent, I agree fully that the CSA must have the ability to have oversight or certain degree of control over critical computers or systems, even if it is located overseas.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But if the "hardware" is out of our jurisdiction and systems can operate virtually without physical boundaries, how will the CSA work with international entities and networks to enforce this?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Compliance is essential but it comes at a significant cost for all entities, government or non-government.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This includes establishing frameworks and processes, investing in and implementing systems, ensuring a workforce that is rightly skilled and potentially high opportunity costs due to extended time-to-market.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These costs can be exacerbated by the rapidly changing operating and regulatory environment, leading to anticipated revisions in legal and regulatory obligations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Educating new entities that will now be regulated by this Act and existing entities facing new requirements must therefore also go hand-in-hand with the passing of this amendment Bill.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How will the CSA and Government calibrate its implementation approach, drive greater awareness and buy-in amongst stakeholders?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It also ensures that the CSA has better situational awareness and stays "on top of things".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But just as importantly, this is a chance for all stakeholders, directly involved or otherwise, to appreciate the dynamics and risks of our operating environment, be vigilant and take proactive steps to keep Singapore cyber secure.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This includes the broadening of oversight across newly classified critical information infrastructure and the introduction of stringent compliance and reporting requirements all aimed at addressing the escalating challenges within our digital environment.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In this age of digitalisation, cyber-attacks on critical infrastructure can pose a significant threat to our national security and well-being.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In December 2015, Ukraine experienced a significant cyber-attack targeting its power grid which resulted in widespread electricity outages across several regions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This was one of the first known successful cyber-attacks on a power grid.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The attackers, who are sophisticated and well-coordinated, used phishing schemes to install malware on the networks of several regional electricity companies.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They were able to gain control of the companies' systems and shut down the substations, cutting off power for approximately 230,000 people for several hours.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This incident not only disrupted everyday life, but also exposed the vulnerability of essential infrastructure to cyber threats and the potential for state-sponsored cyber warfare.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In May 2017 the UK's National Health Service (NHS) was struck by the WannaCry ransomware, a global cyber-attack that infected over 200,000 computers across 150 countries.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The NHS faced significant disruption as the ransomware encrypted data on infected machines, demanding payment to restore access.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Approximately, 19,000 appointments and operations were cancelled and patients had to be diverted from emergency rooms, which were unable to access critical digital services.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The attack highlighted the importance of cybersecurity hygiene as it exploited a known vulnerability in older Windows operating systems that had not been updated with the available patches.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Here at home, in 2018, hackers infiltrated SingHealth healthcare system stealing personal data of 1.5 million patients.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This included information like names addresses and dates of birth.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Additionally, medical records of 160,000 patients, including that of the Prime Minister were also compromised.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The sophistication of the attack, the type of data targeted and the resources needed for such a breach suggested that this cyber-attack may have been state-sponsored.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Each of these incidents served as a stark reminder of the chaos and danger posed by cyber-attacks.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They undermined need for robust cybersecurity measures and the ability to rapidly respond to and manage cybersecurity threats, particularly when critical national infrastructure is at risk.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This explicit authority may be necessary in situations where immediate action must be taken to prevent or mitigate a cybersecurity threat that poses a critical risk.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In contrast, the Bus Services Industry Act of 2015 is more explicit in its wording about operational intervention.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Section 30 of that Act grants the Land Transport Authority (LTA) the power to make a step-in order in certain circumstances.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This order allows LTA to take over the operations of a licensed bus operator or appoint a step-in operator to do so.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Bus Services Industry Act also specifies the powers and functions of the step-in operator, such as having the same powers as the original licensee and requiring the licensee to provide access to premises, assets and employees.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Cybersecurity Act is less specific about what the emergency measures and requirements may entail.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This would ensure that the Government has the necessary tools to respond swiftly and decisively to imminent cybersecurity threats.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Does the Minister see it necessary to develop a framework that enables either CSA or DIS to respond rapidly and directly to imminent threats to our CIIs, ensuring that operational control can be swiftly transferred in a crisis?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Having this operational backstop is desirable precisely because cybersecurity attacks have high potential severity and could unfold very quickly.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will require the strengthening of public-private collaboration to ensure the seamless integration of state and commercial resources in fortifying our national cybersecurity infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In addition, CSA will need to ensure it has the necessary expertise to undertake such responsibilities when called to do so.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: CSA needs to be adequately staffed and equipped with the requisite skills and technology in order to effectively manage and mitigate cybersecurity threats.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Such an arrangement will be in the long-run investment in our own capabilities that is worth making, both in defensive terms but also to enable public-private knowledge diffusion.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can the Commissioner take enforcement action outside of Singapore?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These are events that unfolded in less than one day.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Notably, in 2013, the Act was first amended to address the emerging cybersecurity concerns.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Further enhancements in 2018 introduced the concept of CII, empowering the Commissioner of Cybersecurity with extensive authority to combat and manage cyber threats.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The digital landscape has rapidly evolved over the past five years, emphasising the need for our legal framework to keep pace with these technological advancements.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This allows CSA to safeguard our essential services, even when CIIs go into cloud and the assets are not in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Thirdly, the amendments to Part (3)(a) ensures providers of essential services remain responsible for ensuring the cybersecurity of the service it provides even if the CII is outsourced to a third-party vendor.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These amendments, Mr Speaker, are all vital in a landscape where cyber threats increasingly exploit the interconnected nature of digital systems and the supply chain.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They also address the shift towards cloud computing, where many services are moving away from traditional on-premise models.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Bill enables CSA to extend its protective measures beyond CIIs, encompassing a wider array of systems and entities under the broader umbrella of the Cybersecurity Act.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While I support this Bill, I seek clarifications on several points, mainly focusing on: one, the challenges to its implementation; two, the balance between security enhancements and the compliance burden on businesses; three, how do we manage other technologies that could pose an opportunity and also an equivalent cyber threat, such as the use of deep learning, machine learning and AI within CIIs?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Allow me to elaborate on my first point on challenges to implementation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Will CSA be adequately resourced to manage and implement this, given that a lot of the work requires detailed discussions and working arrangements together with the CIIs?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The requirements for suppliers to report cybersecurity incidents also raise several questions.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What type of incidents must be reported and what constitutes sufficient severity?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If a breach occurs in a system used by multiple customers, including CIIs, such as a cloud-based ERP system used by a CII like SAP S/4HANA, does the provider need to report breaches for instances outside of Singapore?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And considering the complex dynamics and varying bargaining powers between computer vendors and CIIs, can we ensure adequate compliance?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The broadened reporting obligations could also impose a substantial compliance burden on CIIs, STCCs and ESCIs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The potential for increased costs and the challenge of securing legally-binding commitment from powerful computer vendors must be addressed.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we strike a balance that ensures robust cybersecurity without overwhelming businesses with regulatory demands?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On my third point, given that these amendments are made to allow CSA to better secure Singapore's most critical systems in light of recent technological advancements, what is the Ministry's principal approach on the use of machine learning, deep learning and generative AI for CII owners?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is not unthinkable that, given the large amounts of data generated and consumed by CII owners, CII owners may have already begun to explore the use of machine learning and deep learning to optimise their processes.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we ensure that this does not create or open up a potential cybersecurity threat for CIIs?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This Bill is a step forward towards safeguarding Singapore's cyberspace by updating our legal framework to address contemporary challenges.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It aims not only to protect our most critical systems, but also to secure a wider spectrum of digital infrastructure and services.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Notwithstanding the clarifications above, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: More recently, the personal information of parents and staff of 127 schools was accessed due to a data breach linked to a device management app installed on personal learning devices used by students.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Based on the Singapore Business Federation (SBF) National Business Survey 2023-2024, cybersecurity concerns, including increase in cyber-attacks, were a top trend that businesses expect to impact them in the next 12 months.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In this context, the Government's proactive review of the Cybersecurity Act is a welcome one, which will keep pace with our evolving cyber threat landscape and business environment.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: However, Singapore businesses have some concerns about the potential impact of these proposed amendments.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: First, we seek clarity on the criteria and processes involved in designating entities as FDIs, ESCIs and STCCs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: How will businesses be informed about their designation and what is the redress process for companies to review and appeal these designations?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This is crucial for businesses to understand their obligations and plan accordingly, as additional processes and resources will have to be committed to comply with the responsibilities of designated entities.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Second, considering the provisions under the Bill's Part 3(c), which detail the designation of ESCI, there is a need for clearer definitions.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Many companies in Singapore operate computers that store sensitive information and could potentially fall under the broad criteria for ESCI designation.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This includes concerns about what constitutes sensitive information and what level of disruption might be deemed to significantly impact aspects, such as Singapore's defence, foreign relations, economy, public health, public safety or public order.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Given that the list of designated ESCIs will not be published, businesses could be left without clear benchmarks, potentially leading to unease about being designated as an ESCI.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It is crucial, therefore, that we refine our definitions and guidelines concerning these designations to prevent undue worry.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Third, while recognising the importance of enhancing cybersecurity, we must also acknowledge the additional compliance burden these new regulations will impose on our CIIs and designated entities.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We urge the Government to work closely with businesses to operationalise the incident reporting requirements in a streamlined and cost-effective manner.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Fourth, the Bill does not cover standards for mandatory incident reporting or new duties on CII operators.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We should ensure that these standards are developed together with industries before implementation.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Fifth, I would like to clarify if the Bill's intent is to cover personal information only and seek clarification whether the scope of the Bill will be expanded to cover other types of confidential business information?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, we would like to understand how the proposed monitoring powers for the Commissioner and Licensing Officers will be exercised and what safeguards will be put in place to prevent any misuse or abuse of these powers?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: While acknowledging the need for regulatory oversight, we must ensure that these monitoring activities do not impede business operations or compromise sensitive data and trade secrets.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In the next part of my speech, I would like to turn to the pressing issue of cybersecurity within our small and medium enterprises (SMEs).

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: These findings highlight that SMEs are particularly vulnerable and that there is an urgent need to help SMEs strengthen their cybersecurity readiness, as they may lack the resources and expertise to do so effectively.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As the amended Cybersecurity Bill comes into effect, businesses, especially SMEs, along the value chain will need to develop resources and capabilities to report incidents while managing their operations effectively, promptly and accurately.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We therefore encourage the Government to look into providing funding for qualified SMEs to beef up their cybersecurity posture and capabilities.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: There is also scope to look into how trade associations and chambers (TACs) can collaborate with SkillsFuture Singapore to encourage and incentivise businesses to equip their employees with basic cybersecurity knowledge.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: At the individual level, our Government can also encourage mid-career workers to use the recent top-up in SkillsFuture credits to receive training on cybersecurity to ease the talent crunch in the cybersecurity domain.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In January this year, during the "Inclusive and Safe Digital Society" Motion, I spoke in Parliament highlighting in addition to capability building, SMEs also need actual and urgent support in the event of a cybersecurity attack.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As we have discussed today, the vulnerability of businesses, especially SMEs, to cyber threats, coupled with their often-limited resources, highlights the critical need for a change in approach.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our businesses are also even more interconnected worldwide with data transfers occurring at a click of a button.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At the user front, we, of course, have well-known issues of scams and hacking threats and at a wider infrastructure level, there is even greater vulnerability.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our CIIs are inherently vulnerable and that renders them susceptible to a myriad of cyber threats.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Imagine, if you will, the intricate web of interconnected systems that underpin our essential services sector, from energy, water, banking and finance, to healthcare, transport, infocomm, media, security and emergency services and, of course, here, Government.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Envision the catastrophic consequences that could ensue if these systems fall prey to malicious actors.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Consider, for instance, the potential ramifications of a cyber-attack targeting our energy grid.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With our reliance on electricity pervading every aspect of our lives, including right here in this Chamber, from powering our homes to fuelling our industries, the disruption that would be wrought by such an attack would be nothing short of devastating for our economy.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We need only to look at history for precedents.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With cyber-attacks on energy infrastructure in Ukraine that various Members have raised and elsewhere, serving as stark reminders of the vulnerabilities that plague our interconnected world today.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Likewise, our financial institutions stand as prime targets for cyber criminals, seeking to wreak havoc on our economy.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With the click of a mouse, hackers can infiltrate banking systems, syphoning funds and destabilising markets with alarming ease.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The recent spate of ransomware attacks targeting financial institutions worldwide serve as a sobering testament to the gravity of this threat, with billions of dollars at stake and the livelihoods of countless individuals hanging in the balance.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But perhaps most concerning of all of this is the potential for cyber-attacks to compromise our healthcare infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In an era defined by a global pandemic, our healthcare systems have become more vulnerable than ever to malicious actors seeking to exploit weaknesses for their own gain.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: From ransomware attacks crippling hospital operations, to the theft of sensitive patient data, the stakes could not be higher when it comes to protecting our healthcare CIIs.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These examples merely scratch the surface of the myriad of threats facing our CIIs.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: From transportation systems to Government agencies, no sector is immune to the perils of cyber warfare.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As we stand on the parapets of a digital age defined by unprecedented connectivity and innovation, the time is now for us to take decisive action to safeguard our nation's future.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Since the introduction of the Cybersecurity Act, the CSA has had time to operationalise and learn and continue to evolve its methods to prevent attacks on our CIIs.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And so, with this hindsight, we are able to come before this House to debate the amendments that are before us.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For many users, even individuals like ourselves, the ease of access to the cloud makes security challenges even more stark.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Information and data is widely available and, of course, vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Behind all of this is an alphabet soup of GDPR, HIPAA, PCI, DSS, PKI, DNS, HMSs – many of which the end user is unaware of and perhaps does not even understand.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But all these are critical to help to keep our data safe.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, while the amendments before us today largely require CII organisations to ensure compliance, it is also imperative that we educate end users on the importance of data security.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: By bolstering accountability, expanding regulatory frameworks and empowering our CSA, we can pave the way for a safer, more secure future for generations to come.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, Mr Speaker, I support the amendments to the Bill.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Global communications firm Edelman's Trust Barometer survey in 2023 recorded Singapore respondents as having higher trust in Singapore institutions, particularly the Government as an institution.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Nonetheless, the same survey revealed respondents' worries of harm by hackers and/or technology.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: As the requirements appear to only hold CII owners responsible downstream, the Government could also consider articulating efforts upstream, to strengthen trust between the public and CII owners, especially when CII owners race ahead in AI and technology frontiers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Dr Gillian Koh, a senior research fellow at the Institute of Policy Studies pointed out the trust gap in her response to media outlet TODAY Online's coverage of the Edelman survey.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: I quote, "Unless you are younger, more tech-savvy, interested in innovation and have a positive outlook on science and technology, the mass base of people feel threatened by that sort of change." The Bill is in the right direction and can be reinforced by measures that boost CII owners' accountability and transparency to the public.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: I thus seek the Government's consideration of these measures.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: First, the Government could make explicit CII owners' duty to the public.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Such guardrail would raise the public's confidence that CII owners would balance profit motivation and public interest.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Second, the Government could reinforce existing alliances and establish new alliances for cooperation in cybersecurity.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: One, at the inter-governmental level because security threats can span borders.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The ASEAN cybersecurity cooperation strategy is a progressive approach.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Two, at the technology-producer level, because cyber resilience must guide technology product development from the outset.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This would reinforce technology producers' duty to buyers that include CIIs as well as end-users like the public.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Three, at the firm level, because regular information sharing between the Government and firms must be part of the efforts to counter cyber threats.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Such public-private cooperation could be facilitated by proactive knowledge sharing and innovative collaboration.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Insights gleaned from stress tests could be shared with other CIIs, Institutes of Higher Learning and through public reports.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This would set in motion a virtuous cycle for continual uplift in worker training as well as job and research programmes.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Innovative public-private collaboration could be modelled after the Singapore Police Force's collaboration with various banks to stem scams.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Officers from these banks' anti-scam teams are stationed at the Police Anti-Scam Centre and work quickly and closely with the Police to curb scams.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: To conclude, these measures of accountability and transparency would communicate that CII owners, together with the Government and core stakeholders, are active in safeguarding public interest against cyber threats.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: More important, these measures would reinforce the trust among the public, CII owners and the Government that is core to the Cybersecurity (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In 2021, there were more than 2,700 cases reported, with about $5.8 million in losses.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For example, the Singapore Police Force's Anti-Scam Command was established in 2022 to consolidate expertise and resources to combat scams.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Act also allows authorities to order the swift blocking of fraudulent accounts or content, to protect other users from falling victim to scams.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The fact that we are still seeing a rise in e-commerce scams shows that criminals online have the resources to update their scam toolkit to stay ahead of law enforcement in conducting their criminal activities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: According to the annual complaint statistics by the Consumers Association of Singapore (CASE), the number of consumer complaints relating to e-commerce transactions has been rising year on year.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This was followed by an increase of about 14.7% from 2021 to 2022, and another spike of 47% in 2023.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This trend reflects the change in consumer purchasing behaviour.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We now live increasingly digital lives and it is now the norm to work, shop and play online.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We must, therefore, better protect consumers in the digital space.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Obligations include adhering to cybersecurity codes and standards of practice, as well as reporting prescribed cybersecurity incidents to CSA.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Data centres are a prime target for malicious actors because of the sheer disruption it could cause.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: According to a 2023 article on CIO World Asia, a cybersecurity breach at data centres can affect major cloud service providers and the customers who use their services.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Such an attack can interfere with CIIs, impact our digital society and cause serious consequences.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Does CSA intend to adopt any international standards to reduce compliance costs to businesses, which would invariably pass such costs to consumers?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In securing our digital infrastructure, we must strike a right balance between cybersecurity requirements and the impact that these requirements have on the usability of our IT systems.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Many organisations today incorporate the notion of an air gap in their computer systems, as part of their cybersecurity measures.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Air gaps isolate critical systems from unsecured networks, like the Internet, to prevent unauthorised access.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, such cybersecurity controls will sit at odds with the usability of the IT systems.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The greater the control, the less usable the system would be from the user's perspective.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Even air gaps are vulnerable to penetration, as it gives users a false sense of security.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In fact, a quick online search will reveal many examples of data exfiltration techniques designed to penetrate air-gapped systems.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: According to some cybersecurity experts, malicious actors are also increasingly relying on the age-old method of using USB devices infected with malware to attack air-gapped systems, such as operational technology networks.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Without compromising on our cybersecurity measures, I would like to ask how CSA intends to protect our CIIs from such security vulnerabilities while ensuring that cybersecurity requirements are not overly onerous to the point where workers and users find our IT systems unusable.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Imagine if a malicious actor messes with the ability of our Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) train doors to open and shut; worse still, if a cyber-attack on our power grid causes a nationwide blackout.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Such attacks on key ops-tech systems have happened.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In the United States, the Colonial Pipeline ransomware attack in 2021 resulted in a widespread fuel shortage across the entire country.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Any successful attack on our ops-tech systems would, without doubt, result in a significant loss of public confidence in our key public infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, the penetration of such systems can be extremely hard to detect.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
