text: A malicious actor may test its malware by repeatedly causing nuisance, for example, by constantly creating door faults on an MRT train.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Today, we would more than likely treat it as a technical issue, possibly checking that all the electrical wiring and sensors for the MRT doors are in order.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But what if it was caused by malware?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: When, if ever, would we realise something like this has occurred?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Could the persistent issues faced by our banks and telecommunications companies, pertaining to their reported service outages in recent weeks and months, have been a cyber-attack on their ops-tech systems?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I hope that CSA could look into this and build up the necessary capabilities to address these threats.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While remote and flexible work arrangements are a boon to workers, it does create additional cybersecurity penetration points for malicious actors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The proposed changes in the Bill will help to expand the toolkits in the Cybersecurity Act to allow CSA to keep pace with cyber malicious actors and help secure our digital landscape.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Even as we impose more security requirements, we must have a care on the impact that it has on the usability of our IT systems, particularly for those working in our CIIs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We must also build up our capabilities to investigate operational technology faults with a cybersecurity lens.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses are increasingly reliant on digital technology, including cloud-based systems, and cyber threats are becoming more frequent, more sophisticated and of increasing risk to critical industry and infrastructure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The proposals contained in this Bill will enable us to better keep pace with these changes and will enhance our ability to protect critical infrastructure, strengthen oversight of cybersecurity practices and promote closer collaboration between the public and private sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: These obligations will apply to all owner-operated and third party-operated providers, both here and overseas.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Both of these proposed amendments are sensible and will enhance our ability to protect ongoing service delivery of CII in Singapore, regardless of whether the provider of that service is locally based or overseas.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: By broadening the scope of entities, we are better placed to monitor and protect the provision of important or essential services and to reduce potential threats to these services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Before I do so, I should declare that I work in a university – Singapore University of Social Sciences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: First, has the Ministry taken into account the capacity of service providers to meet the new obligations?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: There may also be technical challenges and financial implications for some providers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It may be useful for the Ministry to undertake an engagement campaign, alerting providers to the new obligations and offering technical, practical and financial support or advice as needed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is important that providers move towards full compliance as soon as possible, yet do not jeopardise their business operations in the process or introduce new systems that are unknowingly non-compliant.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It may also assist if the Ministry were to strengthen the existing Cybersecurity Agency toolkit to include a how-to guide that outlines in simple terms what needs to be done and where to obtain further support or advice.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Such a guide could also contain information about reporting obligations, including examples of what constitutes a reportable cybersecurity incident and how to report such incidents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This approach recognises that while these entities are important, they do not carry the same level of risk as CII providers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Without clear and objective definitions, there is a risk of subjectivity in designating entities as ESCIs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This could lead to inconsistencies in regulatory decisions and create uncertainty for businesses operating in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: There is also a need to strike a balance between regulatory oversight and fostering innovation in research and development in the digital sphere.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: While safeguarding critical infrastructure and sensitive data is paramount, overly burdensome regulations may stifle the very innovation Singapore relies on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is, therefore, important that we remain vigilant to the need to protect our society and economy from cybersecurity threats without hindering the growth and development of the digital economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that CSA provides a security bulletin based on the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology's (NIST's) National Vulnerability Database (NVD).

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I also understand that the Infocomm Media Development Authority encourages researchers to submit vulnerability reports.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I would welcome advice about whether the Ministry intends to further strengthen this sharing of information with related entities and the general public by promoting the development of a robust vulnerability database contextualised to Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: A local publicly accessible vulnerability database would assist providers in Singapore to report threats that they become aware of and keep up to date on other threats that may impact on their security and service delivery.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This is sensible and will add another layer of protection of critical personal and commercial information.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I would, however, welcome advice on how the Ministry intends to enforce this obligation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: However, I would welcome advice about what strategies are in place to enable such collaboration without compromising the confidentiality and proprietary interests of businesses and agencies, and without imposing a financial or practical burden on businesses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: By updating our cybersecurity laws, we can better protect our critical infrastructure, enhance oversight of cybersecurity practices and promote collaboration between the public and private sectors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister has rightly emphasised that cybersecurity is a shared responsibility.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It requires the active participation of all sectors of society, from the Government to businesses to individuals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: That is why transparency, clear communication and a commitment to getting the details right are so crucial.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With rapid and widespread digitalisation changing how almost every sector operates, from logistics to utilities, healthcare to finance, we see unprecedented opportunities for growth, innovation and progress.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, such hyperconnectivity also exposes us to pervasive and malicious cyber threats.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For the public consultation on this Bill, there were queries about whether it would be feasible for the Commissioner to require Providers of Essential Services (PES) to cease the use of an outsourced CII in the event the PES is not able to secure a legally binding commitment, given that this may potentially disrupt the delivery of essential services.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The CSA's response is that it would proceed to do so if it has ascertained that the PES is unable to meet its obligations.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This could be due to the highly technical or monopolistic nature of a particular sector.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Regarding the proposed amendments to allow the authorities to designate computer systems of temporary cybersecurity concern due to certain events or situations, would the Ministry share more details about this?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As Singapore is a global hub for key events all year round, it is important to ensure high cybersecurity standards to retain the trust of visitors and investors.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would these powers be applicable to and do the authorities intend to extend these powers to all ancillary or supporting infrastructure, including hotels and event venues, for high-profile or high-level events held in Singapore?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As we work to attract more business and activities to Singapore, we must also stay cognisant of business costs that come with shoring up our cyber defences.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I support the proposed lighter-touch regulatory regime for ESCI and FDI, which will help to strike a balance between increased compliance costs and high standards of practice.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Ministry consider the possibility of industry-wide initiatives that can be rolled out alongside any grants or subsidies, to better support companies in this respect?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):  : As we work to attract more business and activities to Singapore, we must also stay cognisant of business costs that may come with shoring up our cyber defences.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I support the proposed lighter-touch regulatory regime for ESCI and FDI, which will help to strike a balance between increased compliance costs and high standards of practice.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Ministry consider the possibility of industry-wide initiatives – that can be rolled out alongside any grants or subsidies – to better support companies in this respect? : Madam, in closing, I would like to express my support for the Bill.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Let us stand united together in defence of our nation's digital sphere and ensure a safer, more secure future for generations to come.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In March this year, a chamber of commerce in Singapore held a fireside chat with a leading expert on cybersecurity who summarised the threats and challenges for cybersecurity with these words: "The bad guys are here to stay." Simple words, but somewhat scary and that is why this Bill before the House is most timely as not a day passes by in Singapore or any part of the world without a cybersecurity-related event taking place.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Hon Members who spoke before me discussed the need for the various amendments which have been proposed in this amended legislation.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The proposed Cybersecurity (Amendment) Bill represents a significant step forward in enhancing Singapore's digital resilience.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Through these measures, the Bill seeks to bolster our cybersecurity framework, ensuring that we stay ahead of sophisticated and rapidly evolving digital threats.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: With a focus on opportunities for businesses, the amendments provide for market expansion in cybersecurity services, where businesses in the cybersecurity sector can expand their offerings to include services tailored to the new categories, like foundational digital infrastructure and digital service providers.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: There are also avenues for innovation and product development, leading to new patents, intellectual property and leadership in niche markets.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The increased demand for skilled cybersecurity professionals, will provide more avenues for training and workforce development.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This amendment also creates an opportunity for the insurance industry to develop new products and services around cybersecurity insurance, which could become more prevalent and necessary as businesses seek to mitigate the increased risks associated with the new stringent compliance requirements.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: However, these expanded definitions and updated requirements are likely to increase the regulatory burden on businesses and require companies to invest in new technologies.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: For smaller businesses, these increased costs may be prohibitive, potentially leading to competitive disadvantages or even business closures if they cannot afford to comply.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: With the broadened scope of what constitutes sensitive digital infrastructure, businesses must handle an increased volume of sensitive data – raising data privacy and security concerns.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Mismanagement of data, or failures to adequately protect data, can lead to breaches, legal penalties and loss of consumer trust, all of which can have significant financial repercussions.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: We do not want regulatory compliance to unfairly favour established companies.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: SMEs may find it particularly challenging to meet the new requirements due to limited budgets and cybersecurity expertise.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: If they fail to comply, SMEs might face penalties or be forced out of certain markets, reducing the diversity of the business ecosystem and possibly leading to consolidation in certain industries, which could stifle innovation and competition.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Also, the stringent requirements for entities of special cybersecurity interest could act as a barrier to entry for new startups in critical sectors.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Meeting these high standards from the outset could be daunting and financially taxing for new market entrants.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: I have a few clarifications which I wish to raise with the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Knowing these criteria can help companies assess their status and understand whether they fall under this designation.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Organisations need to know exactly what security measures they must implement once designated as STCC.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Also, are there any exemptions or exceptions, particularly for SMEs or startups that might face significant challenges in meeting these more stringent requirements?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In its publicly available closing note on the Bill's consultation process, CSA has communicated that "further industry consultations will be conducted on the development of reporting parameters and applicable cybersecurity codes or standards".

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: To ensure the proposed Cybersecurity (Amendment) Bill is effective and equitable, it is crucial to consider international best practices in its formulation.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: We can draw valuable lessons from the United States, where a recent Executive Order focuses on harnessing AI for advanced cybersecurity; and from the EU's Network and Information Systems (NIS) Directive, which emphasises proactive risk assessment and public-private partnerships.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, countries like Estonia have demonstrated how continuous risk assessment and collaboration can enhance digital infrastructure protection.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: By aligning our roadmap with these global standards, we can develop a robust and forward-thinking cybersecurity framework that not only addresses emerging threats but also fosters innovation and industry collaboration.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It has been almost six years since this House debated and passed the Act; and in that time, technology has advanced rapidly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have witnessed a surge in the use of technology across various sectors, from Government services to healthcare in the private sector.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Unfortunately, this progress has also attracted malicious actors who pose a threat to our security.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Cybersecurity has rightfully taken center stage globally and especially here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is crucial to act swiftly against such threats.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: A robust and regularly updated cybersecurity framework is equally important as our first line of defence.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, DBS and Citibank services saw a complete outage last year due to a technical issue at the Equinix data centre.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While the services were not disrupted due to cyber-attacks or committed by malicious actors, the disruption was palpable and widely felt across the economy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can only imagine if malicious actors were the cause of this damage, it would be wider and more damaging.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Regarding CIIs, owners are currently required to report cybersecurity events involving their systems.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Bill extends this obligation to include peripheral systems connected to the CIIs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This change is crucial as it ensures a comprehensive approach to cybersecurity, focusing not only on main systems but also on peripheral ones, which are equally vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It provides a clear understanding of how cyber threats can infiltrate our networks, promoting transparency and accountability.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, stakeholders have raised concerns about the compliance costs associated with these new obligations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What is the Ministry's current estimation on the increase in compliance costs as a result of the new requirements?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The CIIs also have the option of moving to commercial cloud solutions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How would CSA provide upstream vetting of such cloud services so that the CIIs can have a greater assurance on which are the reliable commercial cloud services.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Would CIIs be restricted to cloud services that are hosted in Singapore only?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Are there concerns on data security of critical infrastructure if these services are hosted overseas?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Moving on to ESCIs, the Bill empowers the CSA to designate and regulate entities handling sensitive data or fulfilling roles of national importance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Maintaining the confidentiality of the list of the designated ESCIs is crucial to prevent targeted attacks by malicious actors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Stricter penalties beyond those provided under the Official Secrets Act for any wrongful communication of this list should be considered to deter potential breaches effectively.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In addition, how often would this list be updated?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Under the proposed amendments, the CSA retains the power to issue written directions to designated entities to ensure cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This sends a strong signal to companies of their responsibility in ensuring cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Balancing cybersecurity objectives with the legitimate commercial interests of entities is crucial, particularly for data centers and cloud service providers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: (In Mandarin):  : We have witnessed rapid technological developments in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Technology has become an integral part of our lives, crucial for the smooth operation of various activities, whether in the Government or private sector.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Unfortunately, malicious actors have caused several data breach incidents in recent years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These incidents have increased by 319% in just the past two years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Government would take action to strengthen our cybersecurity policies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Under the proposed Bill, the CSA will have a broader regulatory scope to ensure our cybersecurity strategies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Regulated entities will be required to comply with directives issued by the CSA or else face severe financial penalties.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I believe that by amending policies targeting new cyber threats, the security of Singapore's cyberspace will be better safeguarded. : In conclusion, Mdm Deputy Speaker, I firmly support the Bill.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singapore has been making monumental strides in its transformation into a Smart Nation.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We are a hyper-connected, world-class, tech-driven state built upon three pillars: one, a digital society; two, a digital economy; and three, a digital government.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In the 2024 Smart City Index published by Switzerland's International Institute for Management Development, Singapore is ranked fifth out of 142 cities.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In the Digital Inclusion Index published by Roland Berger in 2020, Singapore was ranked as the top global leader out of 82 countries.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, the greater our usage and reliance on digital services and infrastructure, the more susceptible we will be to cyber-attacks which are increasing in frequency, scale and sophistication.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Apart from those shared by my fellow Parliamentary colleagues in their respective speeches earlier, this House will also recall some of the major cybersecurity incidents that we have encountered recently.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Clearly, the importance of cybersecurity cannot be overstated.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As a nation, multinational company, SME or individual, we are all vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Upon such designation, would any support be rendered by the CSA to such entity to ensure its familiarity with its legal obligations as an ESCI?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What are the circumstances or the considerations that will go towards publication or disclosure of an ESCI's identity?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Thirdly and related to the preceding point, would actual and potential ESCIs as well as the public be able to access to a database or repository of sorts, in order to review the relevant precedents and case outcomes?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Potentially, such information could be unavailable to serve as valuable lessons, should they be redacted or not reported.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Fourthly, this Bill also introduces a new penalty framework.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To this end, what are the factors the Commissioner may or will take into consideration when exercising his or her discretion over the appropriate penalty to be imposed?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Thus, cybersecurity requires a whole-of-nation effort down to the individual, which must be constantly and diligently performed.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Notwithstanding my clarifications sought, I stand in support of this Bill.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will help Singapore keep pace with the developments in the cyber threat landscape and to ensure that we can continue securing Singapore's cyberspace as well as safeguard our evolving digital economy and digital way of life.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The CII are defined as energy, water, banking and finance, healthcare, transport, info-communication, media, security and emergency services and the Government in the Bill.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I note that a key aspect of the Bill is to ensure that CII owners remain responsible for the cybersecurity and cyber resilience of their systems, while embracing new technological innovations, such as the use of cloud computing and new business models, through higher requirements of incident reporting.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At present, CII owners are only required to report cybersecurity incidents concerning the critical infrastructure and computer systems under their control that are interconnected or communicate with their infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While I understand that doing so will empower CSA to be more aware of cyber threats that could disrupt essential services and work with CII owners to proactively protect those services further, I would like to raise practical challenges that healthcare providers may face.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the healthcare space, entities can differ significantly in operational size and digital capabilities, such as a restructured public hospital compared with a small private general practitioner (GP) clinic.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The question is, whether both entities will be subject to the same requirements under the Bill?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As GP clinics are encouraged to step up to take in more patients under the national Healthier SG initiative, I understand that many are also attempting to digitalise for better operational efficiency.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the higher requirements discourage smaller healthcare providers from digitalisation?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will a more tiered requirement be more appropriate in such a critical sector for our ageing population?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Perhaps, the Government can consider more sector-specific support to help better calibrate responsibilities for owners of CIIs with small, medium and large operations, considering the differing degree of complexity, nuances of virtual systems and third-party ownership in their context.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Another proposal in the Bill is to allow CSA to designate and regulate ESCIs.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, CSA will further create two new classes of regulated entities: ESCI and FDI.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These two classes will be subjected to "light touch" regulations as they are not CII.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Under the Bill, CSA will be able to designate and regulate ESCI for cybersecurity.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The obligations imposed on these entities will not be the same as the levels of those of CIIs.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While autonomous universities have been cited as one example of ESCIs, can the Ministry give greater clarity of what other entities can be designated by CSA to be under these new classifications?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, will a not-for-profit social service agency taking in statutory cases of youth offenders or child protection have any probability of being designated as ESCI?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While ESCI are not CII and the obligations imposed on the ESCI will not be at the same levels as that of the CIIs, will there be guidelines provided by the CSA to give more specifics as some entities, such as smaller not-for-profit organisations may not have the capabilities or resources to bear the additional cybersecurity compliance burden?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Lastly, the Bill also requires companies, such as cloud service providers and data centres to be responsible for the cybersecurity of the digital infrastructure that they manage.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This includes adhering to cybersecurity codes and standards of practice, as well as reporting prescribed cybersecurity incidents to CSA, which will also not be at the level of a CII.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Amendments in section 2, particularly 2(3) and 2(3)(d) introduced definitions of "virtual computers" and "virtual computer systems" as well as defining the "owner" in relation to a provider-owned CII, third-party-owned CII or system of temporary cybersecurity concern that is a virtual computer or a virtual computer system.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Most of these records and databases are uploaded into cloud-based applications, which are increasingly adopted for their scalability and efficiency.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The virtual nature of these assets would mean that physical inspection is often challenging, especially for third-party vendors that operate overseas.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Also, security measures are often under the control and configurations implemented by cloud providers.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, greater specifications may be needed as to how owner responsibility is demarcated from those of cloud service providers.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Worldwide, countries are battling the rising scourge of cyber warfare, marked by an increase in numbers of attempted and/or successful attacks on CII by state and non-state actors.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we have heard already, such attacks should not be taken lightly.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A successful attack on CIIs, say on the healthcare or emergency services, can lead to massive disruptions in medical delivery, potentially endangering lives of hundreds and thousands of individuals.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Admittedly, the outcome of the cyber-attack could have been much worse.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is therefore timely that the Government is reviewing the scope of the Cybersecurity Bill to strengthen cybersecurity standards.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is especially true if their vendors are located overseas or if the infrastructures used by these vendors to provide the required cyber services are located outside of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Stemming from the above question, would the refusal or inability to comply with the amendments to the Cybersecurity Bill automatically preclude vendors from supplying services to CII owners; and would the Government consider such vendors on a case-by-case basis if they are supplying unique critical services that cannot be supplied by vendors elsewhere?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can the Government elaborate on how CSA would work with these CII owners and, possibly, their overseas suppliers and vendors to secure their systems?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And would this involve the possible secondment of CSA consultants to CII owners, their suppliers and vendors to audit and re-design their current cybersecurity system?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would there be funding or support that these companies could possibly tap on to strengthen their cyber systems, bearing in mind that different CII owners, suppliers and vendors could be at different stages of cybersecurity maturity and a one-size-fits-all cyber solution is unlikely to work.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Under the current Government procurement framework, institutions that intend to participate in joint Government projects are mostly required to submit a bid for those projects via an open tender process.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One of the specific amendments in the Bill is to allow CSA to exercise oversights on STCCs and proactively secure STCCs to ensure the cybersecurity of their systems.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the open tender system will ensure fairness and transparency in the awarding of joint Government projects, this would also mean that tender specifications would need to include an extended elaboration on cyber security requirements, which potential STCC vendors might find difficult to meet within the tender period.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is especially so if the procurement of services by STCCs is on an urgent basis, for example, the distribution of COVID-19 vaccine, or something similar.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If the answer is yes, then how would the Government decide which STCC to whitelist and to ensure transparency in the whitelisting process?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My final point is on the ESCI and FDI.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While I can understand the rationale of having a "light touch" approach on regulating ESCI and FDI because they are not CII per se, can the Government, at this juncture, provide more information on how the "light touch" regulatory approach would look like?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Not requiring ESCI and FDI to submit audit risk reports or risk assessments to CSA and not requiring them to participate in national cybersecurity exercises might seem to defeat the purpose of designating and regulating them.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Any forms of regulations, in my opinion, would need to be measurable, of course, assessable and contain penalties for non-compliance.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Singapore's digital economy is the engine of our nation's prosperity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But just as a strong house requires sturdy defenses, our digital realm necessitates robust cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While I support strengthening our Cybersecurity Act, I believe some of the proposed amendments warrant further discussion.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Speaker, Sir, the financial burden on businesses, especially SMEs, must be carefully considered.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need transparency on the true cost of compliance across different sectors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Businesses are the foundation of our economic strength.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We should not burden them with unnecessary red tape.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There are several concerns I want to raise on this aspect.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The amendments may increase compliance costs for these businesses.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The legal jargon may be too complex, something which the public consultation document has itself acknowledged.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This raises concerns for smaller businesses that lack dedicated legal resources.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And the mandatory requirement for CII operators to report all incidents targeting their systems is commendable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With these concerns in mind, I have several questions and suggestions for the Government.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Next, what steps will be taken to ensure that the final text of the Act can be easily understood by businesses of all sizes and the common man?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will the Government support businesses that struggle to navigate the legal changes?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In addition, the Government must ensure that the new CII reporting requirements are clear, concise and do not create an undue burden on businesses.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Moving on, Mr Speaker, Sir, my second topic is on the impact on innovation, which is the bedrock of our digital ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us not stifle it on the altar of security.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must cultivate a cybersecurity culture that prioritises both robust security and a conducive environment for innovation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Singaporean ingenuity has always thrived on calculated risks.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How might the amendments in the Bill affect the agility and risk-taking appetite of tech companies?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In this vein, I urge the Government to elaborate on measures that will be taken to strike a balance.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can we cultivate a cybersecurity culture that prioritises both robust security and a supportive environment for innovation?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The proposed amendments rightly acknowledge the importance of allowing CII operators to leverage new technologies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is critical for Singapore to maintain its competitive edge in the digital arena.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can we create an environment that encourages the adoption of new technologies, while maintaining the highest security standards?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This Bill also has designations like "critical information infrastructure" and "entities of special cybersecurity interest" alongside additional reporting requirements.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will these measures affect Singapore's attractiveness for data centre companies?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Particularly, how will this impact smaller players, subcontractors to larger providers, who may be responsible for third-party owned CII critical to service delivery?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Speaker, Sir, cybersecurity threats transcend borders.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must leverage international collaboration to strengthen our defenses.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Aligning ourselves with global frameworks will enhance our collective response.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For this reason, I urge the Government to elaborate on how these amendments align with international cybersecurity frameworks and standards.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: By aligning ourselves with international efforts, we can ensure that our defenses are interoperable and effective on a global scale.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Government elaborate on opportunities for collaboration with other countries to enhance our collective response to cyber threats?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While this Bill focuses on data centres and cloud servers within Singapore, many service providers utilise overseas facilities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will this Bill address this cross-border aspect?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will providers still be held responsible for breaches occurring in overseas data centres if it disrupts their services in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, Mr Speaker, Sir, the effectiveness of the Cybersecurity Act hinges on transparency and accountability.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This power must be balanced with public trust.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Transparency and accountability are the cornerstones of a strong cybersecurity posture.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The public deserves to know how these measures are being implemented.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Government clearly outline the mechanisms that will be established to ensure transparency and accountability in the implementation of these measures?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will the public be informed about how these powers are being used?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is imperative that we strike a delicate balance between fortifying our national cybersecurity stance and mitigating undue burdens on businesses, especially smaller enterprises with limited resources.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Delving into industry concerns about the cost of compliance, is critical to understand the specific financial implications across different business sizes and sectors to ensure transparency and sustainability.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, providing clear guidance and support, particularly for SMEs, is essential to navigate the new requirements effectively.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, fostering innovation must remain a priority alongside cybersecurity enhancements.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Cultivating a cybersecurity culture that supports both robust security and a conducive environment for innovation is paramount for the continued growth of our digital ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Collaborating with other countries to align with global cybersecurity frameworks and standards will enhance the effectiveness of our defenses on a global scale.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In closing, let us fortify our digital defenses without hindering our economic progress.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With careful consideration and a commitment to innovation, we can ensure Singapore remains a secure and thriving digital hub.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It will update existing provisions relating to the cybersecurity of CIIs and expand CSA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I commend CSA for conducting a public consultation on the Bill and publishing its responses to the feedback provided.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: CSA has also continued closed-door industry consultations and has committed to further consultations in coming up with codes and standards.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have three points of clarifications to raise.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on the legally-binding commitment that designated providers are required to obtain from the owners of third-party-owned CIIs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given that the commitment is provided by the third-party-owned CIIs to the designated providers, in the event of any breach of the commitment, the designated provider is the entity with any right to recourse.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This may be important if the third-party-owned CIIs are not located in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State clarify whether the Commissioner can compel a designated provider to take action against the third-party-owned CIIs pursuant to the legally binding commitment?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If so, can Senior Minister of State also clarify what are the intended actions and remedies that the designated provider is supposed to pursue against the third-party-owned CIIs in the event of a breach?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State clarify how the remedies sought, pursuant to any breach of the legally binding commitment will serve to protect Singapore's cybersecurity?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, will a Commissioner require a designated provider to obtain an order of specific performance to compel third-party-owned CIIs to provide information it is required to provide under the legally-binding commitment?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If the remedy for any breach of the legally-binding commitment is only monetary damages for the designated provider, it may be difficult to see how this will contribute to cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State also clarify how it envisions any remedies being effectively enforced against third-party-owned CIIs that are not located in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on the information collected by CSA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A number of provisions empower CSA to collect information.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, the new sections 17A, 18A and 18H empower the Commissioner to obtain information from an entity to determine if an entity fulfils the criteria for designation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The new section 15(4) allows the Commissioner to carry out a site inspection and audit of a provider-owned CII that appears to be in breach of any requirement.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The new section 29A provides monitoring powers for licensing officers to inspect records of licensed cybersecurity service providers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Respondents also suggested guidelines and safeguards to prevent abuse of such powers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: CSA clarified that the amendments prevent CSA from obtaining confidential information beyond the scope of what is necessary for the on-site inspection.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: CSA also clarified that it would endeavour, where possible, to give notice to CII owners before conducting on-site inspections.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The reality is that what is necessary for on-site inspections can be very broad, depending on how CSA scopes the investigation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is especially since the investigation is for CSA to determine whether the CII owner has complied with any requirement or submitted any false or incomplete information.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This means that the scope of investigation is likely going to be very open-ended.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Giving the CII owner notice before conducting on-site inspection also does not directly address the concerns to do with information collection.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How long will the information obtained be retained for and how will the information be retained?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State also confirm that the power to obtain information does not extend to legally privileged information, and will CSA require entities to waive legal privilege?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third and final point is on the basis for the Commissioner's decisions and beliefs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A number of provisions allow the Commissioner to make orders or directions where it appears to the Commissioner that certain conditions are met.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, under the new section 16F(3), where it appears to the Commissioner that a third-party-owned CII do not meet standards and there is no reasonable excuse for failing to meet these standards, the Commissioner may order the designated provider to cease using the CII.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As I mentioned earlier, under the new section 15(4), where it appears to the Commissioner that a provider-owned CII has not met any standard or provided false or misleading information, the Commissioner can order an audit or on-site inspection.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under the new section 16F(3), where it appears to a Commissioner that a third-party-owned CII has not met any standards or provided false or misleading information, the Commissioner can order a designated provider to cease using the CII.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State clarify whether the Commissioner will provide the grounds of its belief for any decision made or action taken to entities subject to its decision or action?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Gerald Giam, Mr Alex Yam and Mr Darryl David spoke about the potentially devastating impact that a successful attack on our CII could have on the lives of Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Ms Hany Soh spoke about recent major cybersecurity incidents and their serious consequences, while Mr Desmond Choo said that it was crucial that we have robust and regularly updated cybersecurity laws against the increase in cyber threats.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As the cyber threats we face intensify, it is clear that there is agreement in this House on the timeliness of this Bill and the need to put CSA in a better position to safeguard Singapore's cybersecurity.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Melvin Yong spoke about the urgent need to tackle scams.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In January 2024, Minister Josephine Teo spoke about building an inclusive and safe digital society and outlined what the Government was doing to combat scams, so I will not belabour those.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The Cybersecurity Act is not aimed at tackling scams.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Even so, clause 7 of the Bill will allow us to take a stronger stance against impersonation scams, by making it an offence for any person to use CSA's gazetted symbols or representations without the Commissioner's prior written permission.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Melvin Yong also spoke about the need to secure operational technology (op-tech) systems.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The cybersecurity of op-tech is a nascent field, but it is already one of CSA's key areas of work as part of its national cybersecurity mission.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: CSA has established thought leadership when it published the Op-tech Cybersecurity Masterplan in 2019, which is a strategic blueprint to guide Singapore's efforts to foster a resilient and secure cyber environment for our op-tech CII.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: CSA also organises the Op-tech Cybersecurity Expert Panel Forum every year, which is a platform for cybersecurity practitioners, operators, researchers and policy-makers to discuss governance policies, best practices and trends related to op-tech cybersecurity.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The Members who have spoken today have raised several important considerations in relation to the Bill and I would summarise them into three groups.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The first is: are the compliance costs arising from the cybersecurity measures introduced by the Bill justified?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Third and finally, will there be safeguards in place to prevent abuse, as the Bill does expands CSA's powers?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Some Members raised concerns about the additional costs of regulatory compliance: are these costs justified?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Some have suggested that such costs could even adversely impact the community of SMEs in Singapore, or industry development more generally.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: What the Act and the amendments proposed in this Bill seek to do, is to regulate only the cybersecurity of systems, infrastructure and services that are important at a national level because their disruption or compromise could affect our survival, security, safety or other national interests.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is a known and finite set of systems and entities.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Our approach is a targeted and calibrated one, precisely because we recognise that regulation will involve compliance costs.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The first is providers of essential services, whether they are themselves CII owners or rely on third-party vendors for the CII.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Securing the computers and computer systems that are necessary for the continuous delivery of our essential services is a matter of national security and survival.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The second group, comprises owners of STCC where there is a loss of a computer system, or even a system established on a temporary basis would have a serious detrimental effect on Singapore's national interests.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: CSA must be allowed to proactively oversee the cybersecurity of such systems.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is because we need them to be cybersecure if their computer systems contain sensitive information or they perform functions which if disrupted will have a significant detrimental effect on our national interests.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Some compliance cost cannot be avoided where regulation is concerned.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is something we are mindful of and we do not seek to regulate without good reason.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For these four groups, it was a considered decision that we must have the necessary legislation in place to govern their cybersecurity because our national security and other national interests are at stake.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Where essential services are concerned, lives and livelihoods can be affected.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Attacks like these can also indirectly hurt the reputation of the organisation or Singapore.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It can have an external impact on the customers and business partners of the victim organisation.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: These are in addition to potential financial costs.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: These security reasons are also why I had caveated in my opening speech that I will not disclose any specific real-life examples of the critical systems and entities we seek to regulate, which includes ESCIs.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, I seek Ms Ng Ling Ling's understanding that I will not respond to her query on the entities that may be designated as an ESCI.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Ms Hany Soh asked whether there would be circumstances that go toward publication or disclosure of an ESCI's identity – this will be on a case-by-case basis and we must keep the security of the ESCI in mind.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We do not take these decisions to impose obligations lightly.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Mark Lee had the impression that the Bill only focuses on personal information and does not protect other types of confidential business information.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The Cybersecurity Act does not differentiate between protecting personal information and business information as the cybersecurity of all information in a CII must not be compromised.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The Bill will do the same for the new categories of systems and entities we are proposing to regulate for cybersecurity.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Sharael Taha asked about how we asked about how we would address the cybersecurity threats posed by machine learning and generative AI.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The AI landscape is still developing and relatively nascent.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: CSA will continue to monitor our threat landscape carefully, work with the regulated entities to take the necessary steps to protect themselves and address the challenges as the technology emerges and becomes clearer.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Some of the key amendments I covered in my opening speech will allow CII owners to make use of new technologies and new business models.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This can result in efficiencies while maintaining the cybersecurity of the CII.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: These include the use of commercial cloud solutions and demand-aggregated system infrastructure owned by a third-party.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: These could be business opportunities, as Mr Neil Parekh observed in his speech.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: How will CSA ensure that the new obligations are operationalised in a sensible and practical manner?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The technology is constantly advancing and it changes our business and operating context.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They continually find new ways to compromise their targets.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Several members have asked questions about how the amendments would be implemented.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Will CSA operationalise these new laws sensibly and give regulated entities support to meet their statutory obligations?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The short answer to both is yes, but I am going to give a slightly longer answer.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: CSA understands the need to take into account business realities and to be practical and sensible when implementing the Act.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: CII owners and industry stakeholders representing potential ESCIs and major FDI service providers were consulted extensively.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Many trade associations and chambers provided their views during the consultation process.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: CSA's practice is – has been, will be – and is to provide ample support to our regulated entities, by helping them walk towards compliance – walking with them towards compliance.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This begins even before a system or an entity is designated.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Where CSA has reason to believe that a system or entity should be designated, CSA's general practice has been to first engage the system owner or the entity to better understand their operating context, such as the cybersecurity measures already implemented and their level of cybersecurity capabilities, to ensure that any designation is appropriate.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Subsequently, CSA will then work with the system owner or entity to assess what needs to be done for the entity or system to be in compliance with the Act, as well as the support and lead time that the organisation will need.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will only make such decisions after fully understanding the context and how the relevant systems are designed.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: CSA will also consider waivers of the application of a code of practice or standard of performance on a designated entity, where possible, on a case-by-case basis to account for specific operating contexts or the developmental journey of the organisation in question.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As Mr Sharael Taha noted, our CII supply chains are getting more complex.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If a breach occurs to a supply system that is not directly interconnected with or communicates with a CII, the Bill will not require the owner of a compromised system to report such breaches to CSA.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Darryl David asked how we would manage if vendors and suppliers to our CIIs are not directly obliged by statute to disclose cybersecurity incidents.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The principle we apply is that CII owners are responsible for the security and resilience of their essential services.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Doing so would just add the reporting burden to more parties and may not be directly useful for enhancing the security of the CII itself; which ultimately, is what all this work is focused on.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Where the CII is owned by a third-party, clause 14 requires the provider of essential service from the third-party vendor to obtain legally binding commitments from the vendor that would put the provider in a position to discharge its statutory obligations, so that the cybersecurity of the CII is not compromised.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Louis Ng asked several questions relating to how the Government would ensure that we would have sufficient levers against such a third-party.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The intent behind these provisions is to allow the provider of essential service to consider market solutions from third-parties, so that they can be more efficient in the provision of their essential services without compromising cybersecurity.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is not to indirectly regulate these third-parties.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Ms Joan Pereira asked if it would be feasible for CSA to require a provider of essential services to cease using a third-party vendor in the market.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Ultimately, what Part 3A seeks to do is to ensure that providers of essential services who use a third-party's system, in place of operating their own CII, do so without compromising cybersecurity.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Where a provider of essential services faces certain constraints, CSA is prepared to work with them on possible arrangements that could be made.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: However, if there are no solutions on the market that are adequately secure, the provider of essential services should take responsibility for building the CII it needs.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The security of our essential services cannot be and should not be compromised.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In response to Mr Desmond Choo's question on data securities when CII owners move to the cloud, CSA will work with CII owners to conduct cybersecurity risk assessments of any migration of a CII to the cloud.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The principle remains – they must be able to meet their statutory obligations with respect to the cybersecurity of the CII, regardless of the operating model.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The same principle applies to Ms Tin Pei Ling's and Mr Gerald Giam's questions about overseas CII.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Under the new Part 3 provisions proposed by the Bill, the owner of the CII will be held responsible for the cybersecurity of their CII.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It does not matter whether the CII is located in Singapore or located wholly overseas and designated under the new section 7(1)(a).

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Section 7(1)(a) only applies when the owner is in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Similarly, the new Part 3(a) applies to a provider of essential service located in Singapore, who will be held responsible for the cybersecurity of the CII that they rely on.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It does not matter whether the CII owned by the third-party is located in Singapore or located wholly overseas.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The obligations are placed on the CII owner or the provider of essential service in Singapore, so there is no extraterritoriality enforcement of the provisions in new Part 3 and Part 3(a).

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked how we will deal with the cross-border nature of FDI services, such as cloud services and data centre operations.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have designed the new provisions to account for this.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For example, where cloud computing is concerned, it is entirely possible that the cloud services provided to the Singapore market are provided using infrastructure that can be located in any part of the world.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In fact, the ability to tap on infrastructure from any part of the world is a key part of the value proposition of cloud computing because it bolsters the resilience of a given cloud service.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, the focus of our proposed laws is not to insist that designated major FDI service providers report cybersecurity incidents affecting all their digital infrastructures around the world.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng also asked if the designated providers of major FDI service will be held responsible for breaches occurring in overseas data centres if they disrupt their services in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The statutory duties under the Act require the designated provider to work with CSA to prevent and mitigate the cybersecurity risks by, for instance, reporting cybersecurity incidents and complying with the necessary cybersecurity standards and written directions.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Penalties would apply when there is willful non-compliance.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Neil Parekh asked about the types of penalties that could be imposed.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If the proposed amendments are passed, such penalties could be criminal or civil in nature.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum asked how we would enforce the provisions relating to major FDI service providers, if many of these providers are based overseas.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Indeed, this could be the case for the cloud service sector.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Several Members pointed out that some of the operational details are not contained within the Bill.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Matters relating to the technical or other standards that regulated entities must meet and how CII owners should work with the providers of cloud services they use, will be designed to reflect current business realities and prevailing industry norms.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: What the Bill does is to allow CSA to address these in codes of practice or standards of performance and subsidiary legislation, so that we can be more agile in reflecting the operating context.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: CSA will be consulting the industry on these matters, if the Bill is passed.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Many Members like Ms Ng Ling Ling, Ms Jean See and Mr Melvin Yong also gave suggestions on how the Government can provide more support to regulated entities to help them comply with their statutory obligations and provide some assurance that their cybersecurity measures are adequate.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As CSA operationalises the new amendments, CSA will continue to take onboard stakeholder feedback.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Where appropriate and feasible, we will harmonise the cybersecurity standards and incident reporting parameters to be imposed under the Act with international practices.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Gerald Giam asked about step-in rights and CSA's incident response frameworks.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I understand the concern to be whether CSA is adequately empowered to respond effectively to cybersecurity incidents and do what it takes to secure our CII.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Operationally, CSA and the DIS of the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) have an excellent working relationship and will work together to secure Singapore's cyberspace.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The Bill seeks to strengthen CSA's regulatory powers, but as some Members have pointed out, it is also important that CSA exercises its powers responsibly.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Safeguards have been built into the Act from the outset and will be extended to cover the proposed amendments.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: First, any entity that receives a designation notice can appeal against it.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Second, the powers that the Bill seeks to confer on CSA are not unfettered.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For example, the power of inspection provided for in the amended section 15(4)(d) inserted by clause 13, can only be used for the specified purpose and under the specified circumstances set out in the provision.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Third, section 43 of the 2018 Act, which we are retaining, requires specified persons to preserve the secrecy of stipulated matters that come to these persons' knowledge in the discharge of their statutory duties.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This includes information relating to business, commercial or official affairs of any persons and identities of informants.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Section 43 will continue to govern any such information that CSA obtains through the exercise of existing and new powers provided for by the amendments.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling, Mr Gerald Giam and Mr Sharael Taha noted that the Bill will significantly expand the scope of the Act and asked if CSA will be sufficiently equipped to manage this expanded gambit.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: CSA will also continue to develop its personnel and their expertise so that it can continue to deliver its mission at a high level.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I hope that I have sufficiently addressed the queries raised in this House.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The only way we can absolutely guarantee cybersecurity is to not use digital technology at all.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, the task at hand is to find the appropriate balance between security, usability and cost.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The Bill is the sum of the Government's proposal to address this trilemma for the most important systems that affect the national interests.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Where national interests are at stake, the Government needs to proactively ensure that security considerations are optimised.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Those responsible for our CII, STCCs and FDI services, as well as our ESCIs will have to bear some compliance costs, but this is what it takes to keep Singapore and Singaporeans safe and secure in the digital domain.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: That is not to say that their cybersecurity is not important.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As Mr Mark Lee had noted in his speech, confidential business information that our companies and organisations hold are also important and potentially sensitive in their own context.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Our companies and organisations must recognise this and take commensurate steps to address their data security risks.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The Government offers our support to them through other non-regulatory means.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For example, the SG Cyber Safe Programme is a scheme to help the Singapore business community be more cyber secure.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This includes the Cyber Essentials and Cyber Trust marks, which are certification schemes that recognise enterprises that have implemented good cybersecurity practices.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: CSA has also developed the cybersecurity informational toolkits for companies of various profiles, to guide enterprise leaders and their employees on cybersecurity best practices.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Additionally, enterprises getting started on cybersecurity can use the Cybersecurity Health Plans programmes, where consultants help them improve their cyber resilience and help to develop a plan tailored to their needs.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, I urge all enterprises to apply for the various schemes and marks and take advantage of the resources available to uplift their cybersecurity posture.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I also thank Ms Jean See, Mr Neil Parekh, Assoc Prof Razwana Begum and Mr Mark Lee for their suggestions of other non-regulatory initiatives that the Government could consider, particularly on shifting the mindset of stakeholders from one of compliance to one of partnership.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Today, the Government proposes to strengthen our legislation so that we can ensure the cybersecurity of systems and entities that are important to Singapore's national interests.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Cybersecurity is a team effort and one of the important teams are the personnel that we have in our cybersecurity agency.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have been able to attract and retain officers with a high degree of expertise, professionalism and integrity; who are able to balance the considerations of security, usability and cost; who understand and believe in the mission of securing Singapore's cyberspace.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Are there any clarifications for the Senior Minister of State?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Specifically, about the step-in order, I would just like to clarify with the Senior Minister of State whether he thinks that the step-in order of the Cybersecurity Act is on the same scale as the step-in order that is in the Bus Services Industry Act that I mentioned?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Because the Bus Services Act has very specific mention of a step-in function that LTA can order.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: But, I read through Part 4 of the Cybersecurity Act again and I do not see anything that had the same kind of language or the same strength that the Bus Services Industry Act has.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Can I get the clarification from the Senior Minister of State on that?
